name: Maoto (Kampo formula; ma-huang-tang)
short: Case report: maoto-induced interstitial pneumonia. Ephedra weight-loss supplements (not maoto): stroke, deaths; ma huang: 1 liver failure. Licorice: pseudoaldosteronism in Kampo. Studies: none severe.
text: Names and herbs: a 2019 systematic review names maoto (Ma-Huang-Tang) as a traditional Japanese Kampo medicine, and a trial abstract states that maoto granules are made from four plants: ephedra herb, apricot kernel, cinnamon bark and glycyrrhiza (licorice) root. Lungs (case report): a 64-year-old man prescribed maoto for a cold developed high fever, worsening breathlessness and lung infiltrates two days later; low blood oxygen progressed rapidly despite antibiotics, and he then improved quickly in hospital, needing no oxygen by the fifth hospital day; a drug-induced lymphocyte test and a scratch test against maoto were positive, and the authors diagnosed maoto-induced interstitial pneumonia. A 2017 literature review of 73 published patients with pneumonitis caused by Japanese herbal medicines in general (the abstract names other formulas as the most frequent causes and does not name maoto; it says those formulas commonly contain skullcap and licorice, and maoto contains licorice but, as listed in a trial abstract, not skullcap) reports that 13 (18%) needed mechanical ventilation and 3 (4%) died. Studies of maoto: the 2019 review of 2 randomized trials (60 people) and 10 non-randomized studies (1,110 people), which listed side effects and adverse reactions among its safety outcomes, found no severe side effects or adverse reactions reported for maoto or for the antivirals it was compared with, but the studies were small and at high risk of bias; in a randomized trial of 28 adults with influenza (10 given maoto granules by mouth), maoto was described as well tolerated; and among 42 Japanese health care workers given maoto granules for three days after exposure to COVID-19, compared with 13 who declined it, no severe adverse reactions were observed. In a Japanese insurance-claims study of people aged 60 or over with influenza (4,630 matched pairs), hospital admission within 7 days did not differ with or without maoto added to an antiviral, but those aged 90 or over who were prescribed maoto showed a non-significant tendency towards more admissions (9.7% vs 6.6%; P = 0.257), and the authors call for research on its safety, particularly in the oldest people. In children with influenza, a controlled trial in 60 children aged 5 months to 13 years comparing maoto taken by mouth with oseltamivir, and a non-randomized study of maoto in children (its abstract does not give the form), report no adverse-event data in their abstracts. In 21 children with fever given a maoto suppository (a different form from the granules taken by mouth), body temperature fell without serious adverse effects in the 17 who were monitored. Ephedra effects: in 7 healthy adult men, maoto raised blood pressure, heart rate and cardiac output, the strongest effect on the circulation of 6 Kampo formulas tested. A review of Kampo medicines in general lists sympathomimetic symptoms (from ephedra) and pseudoaldosteronism (from licorice) among adverse effects linked to overdose. Ephedra supplements and ephedrine (the abstracts do not name maoto): a review of 140 reports to the US Food and Drug Administration about dietary supplements containing ephedra alkaloids, promoted for weight loss and energy, judged 31% definitely or probably related to the supplements; hypertension, palpitations or fast heart rate, stroke and seizures were reported, ten events resulted in death and 13 in permanent disability; a meta-analysis of safety data from 50 trials of ephedra or ephedrine for weight loss or athletic performance found 2.2- to 3.6-fold higher odds of psychiatric, autonomic or gastrointestinal symptoms and heart palpitations; and a case report describes ephedrine kidney stones (nephrolithiasis) in a person using a ma-huang energy supplement; the authors state that a kidney-stone database shows this is an endemic complication of ephedrine, with hundreds of previous episodes. Other ephedra data (the abstracts do not name maoto): a later meta-analysis of 16 randomized trials of ephedra-containing oral medications for weight reduction found no significant difference in adverse effects between treatment and control groups; the authors note that ephedra is widely used in forms including food supplements and herbal prescriptions, and the abstract does not say which products the trials tested. A review of nephrotoxicity of Chinese herbal medicines, which had no limit on research type, names Ephedra sinica among six Chinese herbal medicines with a risk of nephrotoxicity that had a large number of studies (two studies for Ephedra sinica); the abstract does not describe the harms or say whether those studies were in people. Ephedra and the liver (case reports; neither abstract names maoto): one case report describes fulminant liver failure needing a liver transplant associated with ma huang, which the authors describe as a traditional Chinese remedy containing ephedrine-type alkaloids; the abstract does not say what product was taken or why, or give the patient's age or sex. Another describes acute hepatitis with a ma-huang herbal product advertised for weight loss and energy, which the authors speculate contained another ingredient or contaminant or was misidentified. Ephedra and the eyes (case report, a weight-loss product; the abstract does not name maoto): a 52-year-old woman came to an emergency room with acute pain and reduced vision in both eyes the day after starting a herbal medicine containing ma-huang for weight loss, and was diagnosed with drug-induced angle-closure glaucoma; the authors call bilateral acute angle closure a potentially sight-threatening adverse effect; her symptoms and signs were relieved after antiglaucoma medications. Licorice and potassium (Kampo medicines in general; the abstracts do not name maoto): in Japan's national adverse-event reports for prescription Kampo formulas (4,232 events), there were 1,193 events related to liver injury, 1,177 to lung injury and 889 to pseudoaldosteronism; about 70% of the liver- and lung-injury events were suspected to come from formulas containing Scutellaria root (it is not among maoto's four plants as listed in a trial abstract); the pseudoaldosteronism events, attributed to licorice, included events related to muscle injury, heart failure and arrhythmia; and about 35% of drug eruptions were suspected to come from formulas containing ephedra. A second analysis of Japanese reports found pseudoaldosteronism reported more often with licorice-containing herbal medicines, with risk rising with licorice intake. Outside Kampo, a meta-analysis of 18 studies (337 people) found that regular intake of products containing glycyrrhizic acid (from licorice) raised blood pressure and lowered blood potassium, and notes numerous case reports of severe adverse events, including deaths, after chronic licorice ingestion. Pregnancy: in a Japanese birth cohort of pregnant women, use of Kampo medicines containing ephedra (the abstract does not name maoto) for cold symptoms was not significantly associated with caesarean section, preterm birth, low birth weight, small size for gestational age or low Apgar scores. PubMed searches found no report of low potassium, liver injury, kidney injury or heavy-metal contamination naming maoto. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
